utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Always a pleasure to see you, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, may I deal with one preliminary matter. It deals with the next witness. The next witness is, I believe, 73 years of age. He suffers from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Relatively young.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: A young man, I'm glad to say. He suffers from post-traumatic stress. He has been on medication for a considerable period of time. Yesterday he saw the doctor and nurse because he was feeling unwell. He's available, clearly, to commence his evidence today and he was to arrive at 3.30. I've spoken to my learned friends. I'm told that they may not conclude today or they may conclude today; it's on the cusp of timing, if I may put it that way. I don't know if the Court would object to this defendant not starting -- this witness starting his evidence this afternoon but to start clearly on the Monday. Can I say, however, he is available to commence, if necessary. I only make the application because of concerns for his health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It -- in the circumstances, even though I'm confident the Defence will be quick in their cross-examination, I think it would be an appropriate thing, in view of the condition and age of the witness, to say that we will commence on Monday with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very kind of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence still applies, of course. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. Before I continue with my examination, I would just like to remind you of what we said yesterday, and that is that you should pause before beginning your answer after I complete my question, and I will also pause after you give your answer so that the interpreters could finish their interpretation and so that your voice is not picked up by my microphone. Thank you. Yesterday we talked about it and you explained to us in detail the laying down of mines in Vukovar in 1991. I would just like to ask you a couple of things about that, and that is: Could you please tell us in how many places in October 1991 was the Nova Ulica, Nova Street in Vukovar, booby-trapped, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My second question about this concerns the trip that my colleague showed to you in photographs yesterday -- actually, the road. That is the road from the barracks to the hospital which goes along the Sajmiste Street, Krasova Street, Zmajeva, Dimitrija Tucovica, all the way until the Zrtava Fasizma Square, as well as the Gunduliceva Street. Can you please tell us in how many places was this route booby-trapped in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to correct it. It's Marko Oreskovic Square, not square Zrtava Fasizma. But I didn't understand your question properly. Maybe you can repeat it and be more clear without actually mentioning the names of the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I just mentioned the streets so that it would be clear to the Chamber. In how many places was this route from the hospital blocked or booby-trapped in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In October, only Krasova Street was booby-trapped.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about November?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only Krasova again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will not dwell on this topic any longer. Can you please tell us whether in 1991 you personally knew Stanko Vujanovic and Miroljub Vujic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew those persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know a person by the name of Dusan Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That name is not familiar. Maybe I knew a person of similar-sounding name, but I really can't tell judging just by this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have an intervention for the transcript. It's at page 3, line 14. The last name is Miroljub Vujovic. Do you know that as early as September 1991 there was the logistics and the staff of the so-called Serbian Territorial Defence of Vukovar located at Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As we mentioned Velepromet already, yesterday you told my learned friend while looking at the photograph, which was tendered as Exhibit 250, you pointed out a part of the area where you can see Velepromet, the brick factory and Vupik. Can you tell us how far Vupik and Velepromet are, how far apart are they? Can you give us an estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it would be a distance of about 100 or 200 metres. These two buildings are very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the beginning of the war in Vukovar, both the brick factory and Vupik operated normally. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which period you're talking about. I really am not able to comment on what was normal and what was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether the brick factory was an independent enterprise and did it have any other facilities or buildings in Vukovar other than the ones shown in photograph 250?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not really an expert on this business or economic sector, but I assume that it was an independent manufacturing and merchandising entity and it was only in that one location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please be shown Exhibit 250 on our monitors. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see the photograph that you marked yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Vupik is marked by the letter A, the brick factory is marked by the letter C, and D is marked by the letter -- Vupik is marked -- Velepromet is marked by the letter D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Now we see a part of Velepromet -- one part of it. The other part of it is not visible. Can you please tell us if Velepromet had an administrative building as well as a hangar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you thinking of that location or are you thinking of the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm thinking of this location here.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the administrative building was there or whether it was in the centre of town. The hangars were here, in any case, at this location.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you remember, can you please tell us in relation to this building marked by the letter D here, are the hangars left of this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are actually along the length of the building, further along, to the left side, if you can put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could we say that it was opposite from the Vupik and the brick factory buildings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those three companies formed a sort of triangle.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In any case, we are not able to see the hangars on this photograph, are we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We won't be needing this exhibit anymore. Could you please now show us Exhibit -- actually, it's a photograph with the ERN number 04672115. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you see this photograph and is Velepromet depicted on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This should be the Velepromet in Vukovar at the Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell me whether the building which you marked in Exhibit 250 with the letter D indicating the Velepromet facility, is that this building that we can see in the lower centre of the photograph that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe yes, maybe no. I'm not really sure because I was marking the area; I wasn't marking a particular building, just the area where this company called Velepromet was operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you please tell me whether this area that we can see where the hangars are and the area behind the hangars is an area that is not visible on the previous photograph that we looked at, which was Exhibit 250.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've already said that I assume that, but I cannot state that definitely because these are two separate photographs which can depict different things. So it's not so easy to be specific about which building goes where.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand your caution, but I'm going to ask you this question in this way. Do you agree that in this photograph you cannot see the facilities belonging to Vupik or to the brick factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender this photograph as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Since the Defence wanted to be as efficient as possible, we have divided up our topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So now we're going to move to the actual events in Ovcara, while my colleagues from other Defences will ask you about other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You mentioned you knew Miroljub Vujovic and Stanko Vujanovic. Did you see these people at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see with certainty that I did see Miroljub Vujovic in the hangar itself. And as for Stanko Vujanovic, because of the passage of time, I'm not actually sure whether he was in front of the hangar or not, but I repeat again that I'm sure about Miroljub.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you remember how Miroljub Vujovic was dressed when you say you saw him in the hangar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to what I remember, he was wearing some sort of military clothing and he had an unusual hat, like a commando would wear. It was not something that a regular soldier would wear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that he was wearing some kind of uniform. Was that an SMB uniform, an olive-drab coloured uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a lot of time has passed since then and I recollect that it was that colour. I remember it well enough that it could have been the olive-drab colour, but again I say I cannot be quite certain about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time in 1991, did you also know a person called Ivica Husnjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you see him on the 20th of November, 1991, at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recollect seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you know a person called Boza Vratinovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see him at Ovcara on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall seeing him at Ovcara. His name, though, is Bozo Latinovic, not Vratinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your help. It was a mistake in the transcript. In response to my learned friend's question, you said that you came to Ovcara from the barracks in the third bus. Can you recall what time it was when you set off from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was approximately 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the buses stopped in front of the hangar and that you needed ten minutes -- ten minutes passed from the time you arrived until you left the bus. Can you please tell me if the buses emptied one by one and then left, or were they all emptied at the same time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The buses were emptied one by one, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And a bus that was emptied, I assume, would leave and then another one would come in its place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in response to my learned friend's question that you estimate that about 300 people were brought to the Ovcara hangar, but you made this assessment by multiplying the number of buses with the number of seats in each bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not only by multiplying. This was an estimate -- I mean, I want -- I looked at how many people there were in the hangar and then used this method to get to an approximate number of people who could have been placed in that space.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I assume that in the circumstances that you described in the hangar, you were actually not able to count the people, it was just an estimate of yours, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the question, what was my estimate. So it was an estimate, and I explained how I came to that estimate. I was inside and I was also in the bus. I could see in front -- buses in front of me and behind me that were packed, and then in the space itself I saw how many people were inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you spoke about some people whom you saw at Ovcara, you said that some of them took part in the armed combat, that they were defenders of Vukovar. I wanted to ask you about some people about whom you didn't say anything. So could you please tell us whether Mr. Krizan; Mr. Samardzic, Damjan Samardzic; the gentleman with the nickname Kemo; and Mr. Djukic, Dado Djukic, were the defenders also? Did they take part or were they members of the armed forces that were defending the town on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as these four are concerned with the exception of Kemo, I did not see if Kemo was involved or where, I can confirm in relation to these other men that they did, indeed, take part in Vukovar's defence, each in their own way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: That's why I asked about these four men as a group, just in order to save time. You say at one point your names were recorded by a person in uniform. And having compiled this list, the person left the hangar. Furthermore, you say that inside the hangar you saw a green desk, the sort used in schools. You say that the person who recorded your names approached each and every one of you to ask for information, for personal details. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned that there was a person who recorded our names, but I don't remember mentioning this person leaving the hangar or that room. It is a fact, however, that this military person compiled a list of all the people inside that room.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. But what would you say if I put it to you that a number of witnesses claim that the names were recorded by a member of the 80th Motorised Brigade from Kragujevac who was wearing an olive-drab uniform and that he was seated at this desk that you have told us about. People approached him and he took their names down. It wasn't he that was going around the hangar approaching people, it was the other way around. What would you say about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it may as well have been like that. I'm telling you about my experience, I'm telling you about how my name was recorded. Maybe some other people's names were recorded in this way, but I simply can't speak about that. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You described a person carrying a whistle in the hangar as a rather robust, stout man. When you say said he was stout or big, did you actually mean fat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could put it like that. He was a little on the fat side, of strong build.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Aside from this man with a whistle, did you see a lady wearing an olive-drab uniform inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know this lady from Vukovar? If so, what was her name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Her name was Gordana Karan, and she was from Sajmiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: She was a resident of Vukovar, wasn't she?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Another correction, it's not Kadan, it's Karan, K-a-r-a-n. And the answer to your question is: Yes, she was a resident, at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you also know her family or just her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew her family generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was any other member of her family at Ovcara at the same time you noticed her?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice anybody else, no one from her family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did she have any brothers? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think she did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief that in the section of the hangar in which you were placed there was no agricultural machinery, but there was a room where they might have been -- where there might have been some. Can you please describe where that other section was in relation to the section in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the far end of the room. If you take the door as a reference point, it was deep down inside the hangar. We were scattered or accommodated, whichever way you prefer, at the other end of the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: There were stacks of hay behind you, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under our feet and, to some extent, behind us, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to know is: Did you actually see any machinery or did you just believe that there might have been some machinery over in that other section of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of time has passed and it's difficult for me to say. I do seem to remember that I noticed a piece of machinery there at the time, but there's no way I can be positive about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand and I don't expect you to say anything that you're not certain about. You did not see a single officer inside the hangar displaying a visible rank, let alone a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel, nor did you ever see a military person of that rank enter the hangar at all. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right. I did not see any ranks there. No person there had a visibly displayed military rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were interviewed as witness in Zagreb in the Kadijevic trial, do you remember stating there that in the middle of the hangar Chetnik paramilitaries were beating people with metal rods, punching them, kicking them? Do you remember stating that sort of thing back then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified in chief that people were separated in groups comprising between 10 and 20 people. These groups were then taken to a military vehicle outside every 10 or 15 minutes. You further claim that the first three groups that you saw were taken away by a person in uniform. Now, what I want to know is: Was this person in uniform wearing any white ribbons? Is this something you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that these people were taken to a military vehicle, and there were no special groups. A column was formed comprising between 10 and a maximum of 20 persons, but that's just a ballpark figure. I would say around 10 people in each group were lined up. And the process was monitored by a soldier. I can't say if we -- if he had a white ribbon or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I imagine you are probably not able to describe his face or his physical appearance, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to visualise now. His physical appearance was average and he was wearing a uniform. It would be less than serious if I tried to attempt to provide a photofit of everybody who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand that, but do you at least remember the person's age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have been about 20 or slightly older.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could it be 30 or 40?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not over 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it might be a good idea to go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, if I were to tell you that certain witnesses who were at Ovcara claim that it took more than an hour to take one group away and then come back and collect the next group, what would you say? You did state, after all, that based on your recollection it took no longer than 10 or 15 minutes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing much to say about it, is there? It's a matter of subjective experience. My watch had been shattered or broken, and even regardless of that, time seemed to stand still. The experience of time was subjective for more or less everybody there, and it's largely a matter of personal perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I understand that. I would like to go back briefly to the list that you marked yesterday while testifying in chief. This is Exhibit 258. It was admitted as 258. If one looks at this list of persons, there's one thing that occurs to me. On the 14th of September, 1995, were you not shown another list by the OTP, a list of people who the OTP claim were taken from the hospital to Ovcara and then went missing there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's possible. I would need to look at that list because there was so much searching and inspection going on that I find it very difficult to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let's leave that aside for the time being, although I could show you the list, needless to say, I just want to make sure first that it's absolutely necessary. What I think about the markings you made yesterday, the discrepancy between the two lists boils down to two names. One name is Dragan Gavric, and the other name is Drago Gudelj. You did not mark out these two persons back in 1995 as someone you saw at the hospital along the way or at Ovcara itself. What I want to know is: What jogged your memory, since we know for a fact that you did not mark these two people out back in 1995, whereas now you did?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just a brief one. In fact, this witness has in the past marked two lists, one with a highlighter and the other with his own -- with his own -- in his own handwriting. And in relation to the one with the highlighter, he did mark the name Dragan Gavric, if we're talking about the same list. So it's a little bit confusing. So it may be better that the list be shown to the witness just to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I entirely agree. I was taking a shortcut, as it were, but if it's no good, I'll change tack. Can I have the usher's assistance, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If it may help the Court, the list that has been marked by the witness with the highlighter is 65 ter number 54, and the one that he's -- another list he's marked with his handwriting is in batch number 57. But I think he's referring to list number 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to know about the two names, not the entire statement, but you can go through the statement now. You can confirm that this is a statement you gave and whether it contains a list of names that you marked.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that this is a list on which I marked the names of people I had seen, but you have to be more specific about the names you want to know about and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll do that, by all means. In relation to Exhibit 258, if you look at this list that you now have in front of you, I notice that you did not mark the following names in the previous list: Dragan Gavric and Drago Gudelj. Have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So what's so contentious about that? I'm not clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Nothing's particularly contentious, but the fact is you did not remember those two names back when you first marked the list, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what the markings reflect, perhaps I just didn't remember at the time. Perhaps I just omitted at the time to mark their names without necessarily wanting to leave them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But this is what my question was really about: Yesterday you marked names on the list provided by my learned friend and you marked two more names than you marked on the original list back in 1995. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should have a psychiatrist or a psychologist answer that question because it's more about how human memory works. It's easier to forget facts than it sometimes appears to us. I don't know what else to say. Some things I remember, some things I just can't. Some things I mislay in my head or forget without necessarily wanting to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So this is a case of spontaneous recollection without being prompted by anyone? Am I to conclude that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what I remember. My memory is my memory. No one prompted me to remember anything in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I shall not be dwelling on this list anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I was just wondering whether -- because there are two lists in existence, just for re-examination purposes, if the ERN number of the list that was shown to this witness could be recorded on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means. This is a list served on us by my learned friends from the OTP, and the reference is, together with the accompanying statement, 00338315 through 00338325.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in detail about jumping off the back of the vehicle and running away. The moment you jumped off that vehicle -- and then you reached this place called Ceric to get some water. Would it not be a fair assessment to say that it took a minimum of two and a maximum of four hours between the point of time when you jumped off that vehicle and the time you eventually arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took several hours for me to leave the area; that much is certain. It certainly took me at least two or three or four hours from the time I jumped off of the military vehicle to run through the cornfields and take a number of paths and roads in order to eventually reach the village of Ceric.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have Exhibit 156 on our screens. If that could be run up for us, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And if you could please use that to mark the trajectory of your own journey from the place where you jumped off the vehicle to the village of Ceric. I understand you can't be absolutely accurate, but please do the best you can. I think the scale should be fine for you to roughly mark the trajectory for us. We don't need to zoom out. If we can get a general view, I think that would be really helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So this line marks your journey. The interruptions are just on account of the pen you're using. You don't mean those to indicate that you broke your journey at those precise points, do you? Thank you. The village of Ceric, can you tell me how far it is from Marinci, if you know, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Say about a couple of kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The same distance from Zidine, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is Zidine? I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Zidine is a place on the road from Bogdanovci to Vinkovci. I apologise, close to Nustar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've never heard of Zidine.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about Nustar, how far is Nustar from the village of Ceric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: One to two kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 263, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us if at the time you knew that Nustar was in the hands of the Croatian defence forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us how you reached Ceric, how you tried to get water, and how you were captured. What I'm interested in is whether you were interrogated there by the persons who captured you about who you are, where you're from, and so on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course they asked me who I was, where I was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I told them that I was leaving Vukovar. I was going in the -- I was going to join my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell them after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that I told them what was going on. I told them all I knew and all I was able to tell them about that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And after that they handed you over to the military police in Stari Jankovci and that's where you questioned by a captain in the military police. I think that that's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the soldiers who had practically captured me took me to their command post, and after a while spent there where I was abused. I was transferred to Stari Jankovci, where I was questioned by the captain, the JNA captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me if the captain knew about your activities in Vukovar at the time you were brought in and did he know where you were coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's a question for him, not for me. I don't know what someone knows or doesn't know. It's a little bit of a strangely formulated question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Well, I agree. But I will ask you in this way. Did he ask you what you did in Vukovar and how you reached Ceric?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he asked me what I did in Vukovar and what was going on there. And I laid my cards on the table, as they say, told him all the things that I did. And I provided a complete statement to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But you didn't tell him that you had come to Ceric from Ovcara, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I didn't mention that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you indicated where the minefields were and you showed him where you had buried all the documents relating to the minefields. Did you go and show them where this place where the documentation was buried or did they go and get that themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't tell him where my documents were, but I explained, based on my recollection, where the mines were located throughout the town, based on my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I obviously misunderstood what you said. Can you please tell me how it came about that members of the JNA found these documents of yours. Did you tell them or did they happen to find them in some other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They couldn't have found the documents by themselves. I told them about it because one of the soldiers during the interrogation said if I had any records of it, where did I leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. This staff sergeant, can you please tell me where you were when he asked you about it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, warrant officer, not staff sergeant.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This interrogation took place in Sremska Mitrovica. It was conducted by the JNA warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. After this interrogation in Stari Jankovci, you said that the military police transferred you to the Sid police station. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, these were the premises of the Ministry of Internal Affairs in Sid.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told us that there you were questioned by a person wearing civilian clothes. Did he introduce himself to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, nobody introduced themselves. He didn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because you were brought to Sid by the military police as a member of the Vukovar defence. You were arrested because you took part in the conflict and, I assume, because of what you were charged with later. So what I would like to ask is: Is it possible that this person in civilian clothes about whom you assumed was a civilian inspector was perhaps from some other structures? How do you know that he was a civilian police inspector?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as my arrest, it's questionable whether it was legal or not. But obviously I was detained by these forces. Whether this was rightful or not, it's another matter. But as far as that man is concerned, it was my personal conclusion that perhaps he was some kind of investigator or an inspector, a MUP inspector. However, I cannot really corroborate that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After this conversation with this person, the military police took you to Sremska Mitrovica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Me and also the people that I came with.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You already told us about that. You also told us about the conversation you had with this civilian -- or this person dressed in civilian clothing at the police station. What I would like to know is whether he was the first one to mention Ovcara and your presence there or were you the one who mentioned it first?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he made that suggestion in order that I would perhaps tell him a little bit more about that -- or rather, he was trying, in a way, to find out from me something more about it. So it didn't come from me first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us how this conversation ended. What I would like to know is whether you, until the time you left for Sremska Mitrovica during any of the interrogations, did you provide any statement, sign a statement, was a statement drafted in your presence, in the presence of these officials as well? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking about the time before Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about these interrogations you had before Sremska Mitrovica, so I'm talking about, Ceric, Stari Jankovci, Sid.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that was written were the notes or the record of the captain in Stari Jankovci, but I cannot recall if I signed anything or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me whether you provided and signed a statement in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did give a statement there and I think that I also signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you questioned by this warrant officer the whole time or were there any other people there during the time you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other interrogators who came from the military investigative prison from Belgrade. They also conducted interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall whether you were interrogated by an officer there, a JNA officer, whose name was Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that -- actually, I don't remember names. There was an officer there who was interrogating me, but I don't know if this was Colonel Branko or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If it's not asking too much of you, do you recall that officer? Could you describe the officer who was interrogating you? Could you describe his build, for example?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was of average height, perhaps with a slightly darker complexion. I don't know. He didn't have any particular characteristics. Obviously he was an officer. He told me himself that he was -- he came to that area after the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what sort of hair that officer had and can you tell me whether you thought him as being thin or fat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't fat, certainly not. He was of heavier build, but he wasn't either skinny or fat. Perhaps he had brown hair, but I really cannot be certain about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your efforts to describe him. Can you also maybe give us his age, roughly, at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 30 and 40 years of age, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you were asked about the events at Ovcara in Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody in Mitrovica asked me about Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that after that you were transferred to the military investigative prison in Belgrade and proceedings were conducted against you which were never completed. I think that that's what you said. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were proceedings, but I really don't know whether they were ever completed or not. I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, that wasn't the gist of my question anyway. What I would like to know is that whether you were treated properly at the Belgrade prison. Were you given the right to have a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As time went along, finally we did -- or we were represented by defence counsel sent by the Republic of Croatia. And he was covering me and the other people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So you were in contact with him and, I assume, also with assigned defence counsel who were assigned to you before that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was hard for me to say. I don't know who got in touch with whom. The proceedings were strange from the beginning of that so-called trial or the proceedings as a whole against us who had to go through them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please tell me whether at the time, did you tell any of your defence counsel, whether your assigned defence there or the ones sent by the Republic of Croatia, about the events in Ovcara? Did you tell either of them anything about that at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not a topic of conversation with them at the time. I did not talk about that with any of the people there at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have another question relating to Sremska Mitrovica. When you were there, did representatives of the Red Cross come there? Were you registered by representatives of the Red Cross while you were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were registered by the International Red Cross sometime in December.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me the following. You were exchanged in August 1992. Do you know who was involved in the negotiations relating to this exchange? Do you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything specific. All I know is that this was the largest and, let's say, the biggest all-for-all exchange. As for who negotiated, who took part in that, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, about your detailed answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic, or would you like to have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't matter to me, Your Honours. It's up to you. Perhaps we can ask the witness if he would like to go on a break. He has been responding to questions already for an hour and a half, but we can also tell the witness that the break would be taken in ten minutes anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think I would agree to go on a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Having had that democratic determination, we will have a break now and resume at five minutes or just after five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Mira Tapuskovic, and I am a Defence counsel, or one of the Defence counsel for the accused, Mr. Radic. I'm going to be putting questions to you now. I will try not to repeat the ground covered by my colleagues or my colleague Mr. Vasic. I will only dwell on something already covered in case I need any additional explanations. The day before yesterday when my learned friend from the Prosecution asked you a question about the weapons you had in Vukovar or, rather, which the defenders in Vukovar had. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You responded to the question that besides light weapons or side-arms -- perhaps I'm making a mistake in this qualification, but I think you said you had light weapons, side-arms, and that you also had two or three tanks and two or three guns. Am I remembering correctly what you stated the other day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was mentioned. Two or three tanks were captured in the fighting and the two guns or several guns, perhaps, we had from before. But I really can't say much more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot hear the interpretation, so I don't know when I can start putting my question to the witness, but never mind. I will try to stick to a comfortable pace as far as the interpretation is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said that those two or three guns were captured by the JNA, they were captured from the JNA -- actually, I'm talking about the tanks. And then you said you didn't know where the guns were from. Do you remember if the Vukovar defence forces at the time also had anti-aircraft guns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are difficult questions for me. I one a commander of the defence or in some higher rank, so I really don't have much information about these matters and I'm not really able to answer these questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I just felt that you as a person who had spent a lot of time on the streets of Vukovar and was in contact with the activities of the defence forces, you would be able to respond to a question like this. But let me go on. If you don't know exactly if there were any anti-aircraft guns there, do you perhaps know if there was a unit like that in the territory of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you followed my testimony and then know that I joined up much later than all of the events from the beginning that were occurring in the defence of Vukovar. I don't really know much about that, but I can make assertions or I can give you my opinions. But I'm not able to make things up here and talk about what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to put the following question to you. On a couple of occasions you mentioned that at Ovcara in the hangar you saw Vladimir Djukic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to put a direct question to you. Do you have information that he was at the head of the anti-aircraft unit of the Vukovar defence forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have information to that effect, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A few days ago we had a witness here who was also from Vukovar, just like yourself.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friends from the Prosecution, that is page 3541 of the transcript of the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That witness told us that there was artillery support from Vinkovci. Do you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just a little bit of information. There was some support from that sector, but again I say that I wasn't at that high level of command so that I would be able to tell you anything that was of key importance and that was absolutely certain.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Your answer is quite adequate. In order to avoid repeating things that were already said yesterday and today, you told us that you were summoned to the municipal building for some sort of meeting and that this meeting was attended by about 50 people and that an agreement was being reached on how to approach the defence of Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a meeting relating to all of the events that were becoming more and more complex, and more needed to be done to assist the defence of the town. So that was the purpose and the sense of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that mobilisation was being carried out. You said that it was ethical, moral, and legal, and that it was implemented for the whole area of the Vukovar municipality. You said that. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this term "implemented." It was proclaimed. I don't know to what degree it was implemented. I'm not sure whether that's the proper term, but there was a -- a mobilisation that was proclaimed for that whole area.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: A mobilisation had been declared, a general mobilisation, you're quite right. Maybe the expression I used was not correct. Did you receive a call-up in writing or was it over the radio, the public media, the TV that you were called to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told to come to the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: People knew at the military recruitment office that your reserve rank was the second lieutenant of the former JNA, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume people knew, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So it was at this time that this unit was set up which was known as a blasters' intervention unit. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it was actually called an intervention unit, but a new unit was set up and restructured. The unit was reorganised, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I used the expression "blasters' intervention unit" because this is something I read in one of your statements and that was how you, yourself, described the unit in your statement to the county court back in 1996. It is immaterial what the name of the unit really was, therefore I will not go any further into that but thank you for your answer. Regardless of this, you became a member of the 204th Vukovar Brigade. In 2003 you were granted membership when this brigade was, as it were, legalised by the Croatian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that I was classified as a member of the National Guards Corps, at least that's what the first and earliest documents that I received about my own status indicated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you some questions about the work of your group. I won't be asking you questions about the procedure of mine-laying or booby-trapping itself, because I think my learned friend Mr. Vasic has already covered that sufficiently. You say that Mr. Borkovic was the one who gave orders to your group. His nickname was Mladi Jastreb. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right to some extent, but there's one thing you need to understand. At first there was Stari Jastreb, and he was at one point succeeded by Mladi Jastreb. First you had Stari Jastreb, who was the original commander; and back then Mladi Jastreb was his deputy. Jastreb was in charge of us, he was our commander. I don't know what appears so questionable about that to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There's nothing questionable at all about all these terms, but can you please confirm for me that both Mile Dedakovic and Branko Borkovic were called Jastreb 1 and Jastreb 2 or Stari Jastreb and Mladi Jastreb respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, "Stari Jastreb" and "Mladi Jastreb" translate as "old hawk" and "young hawk" respectively.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure what you mean. There was a Stari Jastreb and there was a Mladi Jastreb. But sometimes the word "Jastreb" itself sufficed and one didn't need to specify. Whenever one said "Jastreb," one knew immediately that our command was on the line and no further specification was needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just replied that it was quite sufficient to utter the word "Jastreb," whereby you have already answered my next question, which was a question about the existence of a Jastreb 3. But let's leave that aside for the time being. There is one particular place that I wish to ask you about. I want to know whether that place was booby-trapped by using anti-personnel or anti-tank mines. I'm talking about the fly-over near the Kuplijanacka Road [phoen] -- Bogdanovci Road? Did your group booby-trap that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no fly-over there, at least that I know of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5788 yesterday you claim you didn't know where the mines were obtained that turned up in your storage rooms, nor were you aware of their exact quantity. Is that a fair reflection of what you stated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I had no idea where the mines had been obtained, how they got to be there, or how many. So, yes, it's a fair statement on your part.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to refresh your memory about something in your testimony. I will try to avoid having you read that portion. It would be great if you could just remember it without being prompted. At the Belgrade trial when you were an accused you said that there had been over 40.000 mines laid in Vukovar, randomly as well as in an organised way, and that some mines were laid by people spontaneously, as it were, without the relevant orders being given. Do you remember that portion of your testimony some years ago?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that is what I said, that only means that a lot of minelaying had been done before I arrived on the scene and after. This is when accusations were leveled against me and my group; we were the ones who stood trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said this once you were cautioned during the trial that you were not obliged to release any statements or even offer a defence. Do you remember this as something that you said without being prompted to say anything like that by the person examining you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anyone informed us that we were not obliged to answer the questions asked. I remember the trial, but the figures strike me as somewhat arbitrary. They're ballpark figures, if anything. They're just meant to give a general idea of the magnitude of everything that had gone on before I first arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the first day of your examination-in-chief and also while

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: about 1.000 mines. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It's a rough assessment, but there are documents to show how many mines exactly. I'm just not sure how that should be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You say that you only laid mines along the confrontation lines and you also said, when prompted by my learned friend Mr. Vasic, that you laid no mines in private homes or private gardens. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are neglecting the nature of the clashes in the area. The entire town was turned into a battle-field, and at this point there were no private homes or private gardens. The entire place was a battle-field. Life itself became a battle-field. I'm not sure what, under the circumstances, your mind would define as lawful or unlawful in the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, can we now please show a brief video clip. This is an excerpt from an already existing exhibit, Exhibit 136. This is a 16-second video recording. For the benefit of my learned friends, this is DO video V000-4593. If that can please be played for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As I said, it's a very brief video, no longer than 16 seconds. I hope you played close attention. This video was filmed by a foreign journalist, who was also heard by this Trial Chamber. While watching this video, did you perhaps notice someone wearing a uniform poking around among some leaves on the ground with some sort of a stick in a bid to locate a mine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I followed the video closely, but I'm not sure what it represents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's a very short film. We'll play it again, and if I could please ask you to pay close attention to the location and what exactly goes on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, this obviously takes place in the town of Vukovar itself in one of Vukovar's neighbourhoods, in a settled area. Is that not right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What leads you to conclude that this particular bit of action takes place in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I introduced this by saying that this is an exhibit that was already admitted. It was an exhibit tendered by the OTP, and it's about what went on in the town of Vukovar itself, which is not something that you necessarily know about and there's no reason why you should.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, since I have no intention of asking the witness any questions about this video, what I would seek to do is tender this portion of the video into evidence; or, alternatively, I can leave it to the Trial Chamber to decide, since the longer version, the entire version, has already been tendered and admitted as Exhibit 136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I don't think we need it as an exhibit; we have it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, Your Honour, I entirely agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber what is your point about showing the video at this point of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while testifying in chief and while being cross-examined by Mr. Vasic, the present witness spoke about mines being scattered along the front line. He also spoke about the fact that no mines were laid in gardens belonging to private homes or anywhere near any private homes. What we see in this short footage is that there were mines laid there covered by leaves and dirt and that mines were, after all, laid in areas between private homes, houses, and in backyards, and people's private gardens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the witness might like to comment on that, if that's the point of this. I must say I had a different understanding of the effect of his evidence, but I won't say what I understood. Let the witness deal with the issue. I think the point being put to you that if this was in fact a film taken in Vukovar at the time, does this not reveal mines having been laid in a domestic garden? And if so, does that call into question what you were saying about where mines were laid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there is no essential discrepancy between this and what I was saying. Mines were laid along any portion of the confrontation line, and sometimes the line ran between houses and combat would break out in settled areas. I don't think there is necessarily a contradiction to my previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have ruled that there is no need tender this video again, and I have no further questions in relation to it. I do have one question left about this subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, you say that other blasters units and groups existed. Are you familiar with a group called nightingale or another group called mine 1 or yet another group, mine 2?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these all sound unfamiliar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Let me try to jog your memory. On the 11th of August, 1992, at a trial you talked about the existence of these blasters units or groups --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if I could have the usher's assistance for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph, you will see that it's highlighted in orange. The next page, the first paragraph, page 12 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters couldn't hear the last part of what counsel said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This is the military court in Belgrade, a trial where you and two other persons were accused. That was back in 1992. Charges were brought against you and two other persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This reference to something called nightingale here, this is not a blasters unit. This was a defence position. The reference was to a particular defence position.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Maybe I misinterpreted the term "nightingale." Thank you for shedding light on that. Can you now please go to page 12, the highlighted portion. Sir, can you please go through the paragraph that is highlighted in orange. Please read it aloud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. Should I start?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Otherwise we were the only blasters group in the area. Before us there were other blasters units, mine 1 and mine 2. Mine was called mine." Can I tell you what I think about this whole thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you could just hold a second, sir, it's because of the interpretation and I have to make a correction there. I have to set you right, as it were. You misread one word in the second line, and could you please read the entire paragraph again for the sake of the interpreters and for your own sake. You can go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fine. "Otherwise we were the only blasters group in that area, but before us there were other blasters groups called mine 1 and mine 2. My group was called 'mine.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What's your comment now? Back in 1992 at this trial you indicated with a degree of accuracy the names of those blasters groups, which would seem to suggest that they existed at the same time, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's quite obvious that this was stated wherever it was stated, but because I had to re-construct the history of my own activities there, I can tell you as follows. There was a commander in charge of the unit before I came along. I assume and I remember that he told me something about this. These names, mine 1 and mine 2, I don't think are accurate. I think it was Kupa 1 and Kupa 2. I can't be sure about it, though. But what I said about there being booby-trapping and blocking and mines being laid before I came along does not strike me as very noteworthy or special.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Maybe that's what you think, sir, but you also suggested that any minelaying done outside your own group was not done in an organised manner. What I am trying to demonstrate here is that apparently there were other organised groups, just like yours, and these groups had names. And as you have just told us, there was yet another blasters group, a unit, that was commonly referred to as Kupa, K-u-p-a. Thank you for answering the question, sir. You said there was a great deal of trouble in relation to food supplies during the fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would like to go back briefly to the previous question because I don't think we have sufficiently clarified what had been going on with minelaying before I came along. I think you brushed it off too quickly, in a way, without touching on the essence of what exactly happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, for my purposes what has been said is more than sufficient. I have received all of my answers, and no further information on this subject is requested for the time being. But you are yet to be cross-examined by another counsel and maybe there'll be further opportunities for you to say what you know. Let's go back now to the next topic that I wanted to cover with you. I would like to go back to the question that I put to you -- or actually, to the remark that during the examination-in-chief by the Prosecution you stated that there were problems in supplying Vukovar during those three months, September, October, and mid-November, until the fall of Vukovar, there were problems in supplying Vukovar with food. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How could there not be difficulties in a town that was being hit from all sides by numerous weapons? In a town that had been cut -- where -- where electricity had been cut, water had been cut, and where it was so dangerous, in terms of survival, that this even is not something that would have to be explained here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I agree with you that it was difficult to move around the town in view of what you stated today, that at least 40.000 -- or approximately 40.000 mines were laid in the town. What I'm interested now is the problem with the food. You had to leave some corridors for the food supply of Vukovar, and these corridors had to be accessible and mine-free. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your thinking is a little bit strange, but we were not laying down mines in the town, we were doing it on the outskirts of town in order to booby-trap that area to prevent the enemy from breaking through. That was the purpose of booby-trapping and laying obstacles. Life went on within Vukovar. However, it was being supplied from the inside. It lived from the inside. People who participated and lived through that can of course tell you more about that, but of course, needless to say, the conditions of survival were very difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask you is the following: Do you know that during those three months in Vukovar, regardless of the fact that the approaches were mined - and you indicated this on the map that you marked yesterday - food and medicines were still being brought in. Are you familiar with this information or with this fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the extent that you would think. The routes, even if they existed, they were not actual roads. These were side roads. These were paths through cornfields. Alternative routes were used, sometimes even from the air. So we're not talking about just regular transport and roads or normal conditions; we're talking about conditions in a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What would you say if I were to tell you that the Yugoslav People's Army on several occasions made it possible that food supplies reach Vukovar and that these deliveries were recorded in the diaries or the log-book of the Guards Brigade? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of this. Why would I be aware of this? The other thing is that what I know is that there were cease-fires but the conflict still went on, so all it boiled down to was some kind of psychology or second-guessing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But the cease-fires were also implemented in order to facilitate food and medicine supplies, and these supplies arrived by some other routes, not through cornfields. Does that sound logical to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're not talking about conclusions here but about events, and what took place was that there was constant shelling. It never stopped. We're not talking about any cease-fires. There was nothing like that. There was constant fighting; there were no breaks or interruptions. All that went on, the life and everything else, went on under war conditions and under constant shelling, day and night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me that if you say that the shelling went on day and night and that on the first day during the examination-in-chief you said that the town was hit by tens of thousands - and you even said hundreds of thousands - of shells, would you accept the possibility that a large number of mines out of those 40.000 mines that were laid down in the Vukovar territory or along the front lines were detonated in this shelling and that there was large destruction inflicted on the town, amongst other reasons, also because of the way the town was mined in the way it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, that question contains a number of propositions which the witness hasn't agreed to. And firstly, in relation to the 40.000 mines, I think he said that number wasn't necessary an accurate number but reflected the general magnitude of some of the minelaying. And he also hasn't testified to the fact that mines -- of the way the town was mined. He testified to the fact that mines were laid on the outskirts of the town and as the confrontation lines moved in, then so did the minelaying, but I think a number of those propositions are not right and make it a confusing question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, though, the end result of the question was clear enough, which was in essence: Wasn't a lot of the town damaged by the explosion of mines that had been laid by the defenders, if I understood Ms. Tapuskovic correctly, and I think the witness can deal with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can say and add to this is that this construction is not technically impossible. Anybody who is versed in explosive devices would know that during shelling it's possible that explosions occur. However, in this case it really doesn't make sense because these mines that we're talking about now were laid down along -- during a certain long period of time. And the shells that I'm talking about happened in the initial phase, maybe during the first few days, when an indescribable amount of ammunition was fired. I couldn't or anyone else couldn't count how many shells fell in the very beginning of the siege. I'm talking about the 24th or the 25th of August, 1991. So to derive such a construct from what I said doesn't really make too much sense. Scandalous.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours, because of the confusion, but the devices on my right side were not working properly. So I was not actually receiving the whole interpretation at the right time. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In any case you responded to the question that I put to you. I have one more question in that regard. The population that you said was in shelters, can people who are in shelters differentiate between mine explosions, no matter how they explode, regardless of whether a shell that fell exploded the device or it exploded because a animal tripped on it or something else? Can they be certain that a certain sound is a sound made by a shell? Did you understand what I am trying to say? Can a person in a shelter differentiate in the sound made by an exploding shell or an exploding mine? I'm talking about an average person.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question and the attempt to try to confuse those who are listening. I did mention that these shelters were inside the town of Vukovar and were far from the places where there were clashes. So any person in the shelter would easily know that we were talking about incoming shells, not mines that had been laid down and now that they were exploding. In this case, this was not possible. Shells were dropping only from the sky. It was not possible to activate mines there because there were none there. I mentioned before that all the shelters were within the town. They were not out in the places where there were clashes and where mines were laid down.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to move on from the topic of mines and shelling. We're going to move to something else now. We're going to talk about the events in the hospital. You said that you heard in some way that there would be an evacuation and you set off for the hospital together with your parents. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Either somebody brought the news or somehow it spread. It was disseminated. We found out in some way that an evacuation was being prepared, the possibility to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said here that when you came to the hospital approximately at midday, so I make my conclusion that this was around noon, and when you came in front of the hospital you could see an armoured vehicle where there was a major and a lieutenant there?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
