utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the question. Please, could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You told my learned friend from the Prosecution, and also yesterday in response to a question by my learned friend Mr. Vasic, you said that around noon an armoured vehicle arrived in front of the hospital bearing a major and a lieutenant. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was just confused by the abbreviation you moved, BOV, for the armoured vehicle. But I understand what you meant to say, Borbeno Vozilo, armoured vehicle that arrived in front of the hospital bearing this officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I thought that you would know what a BOV was. I just wanted to remind you of the statement that you gave to the Tribunal investigators in 1995. I will help you to remember, and I hope you remember - if not, I'm going to show you the statement you gave to the investigators - that you stated that the face of the person that was on that armoured combat vehicle was something that you recall very well and that it was etched in your memory and that you would recognise the person if you saw anything that would remind you of that person. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember the person and I stand by what I said. I remember that face to this very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask for another brief video footage to be shown. This one is 93 minutes -- seconds long.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23 seconds long and it's from the R65 ter list and Exhibit number 312, and it bears the number V000-687. I would like to ask the witness to listen very carefully to what is said in these 23 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you want us to play this clip again? These are very short clips.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, the vehicle that you see in this clip, is that the type of vehicle you saw that day at noon in front of the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that it was that vehicle, but the person in the vehicle, the major, seems to be that person that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have this clip exhibited? We would like to tender it into evidence because the witness said that that was the person whom he saw in front of the hospital that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think he said it seems to be but not that it was the person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be exhibit number 264.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, now we're going to discuss the events at Ovcara. I would like to take you back to what you said a few days ago here, according to the transcript. This was on page 5728, line 12. I am giving the reference in order to assist my learned friends from the Prosecution. You said that when you came to Ovcara there were many people in front of the hangar, about 50 people or more. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it meant -- it included the personnel, the military and the paramilitary personnel who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Very well. The military and the paramilitary personnel. Do you also recall stating on page 5734 that at that time in the hangar when you entered it there were many locals as well as people who did not come from the Vukovar area? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We talked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether you saw members of the TO units in front of the hangar and in the hangar on that day when you entered the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do you think that I would be able to so easily differentiate between reserve forces, Chetniks, and tell who belonged to which formation?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether you saw them in front of and inside, but if you're not able to tell us that then very well. That's not a problem. What I would like to ask you now is: When you were getting out of the bus and when you were approaching the hangar, did you perhaps see parked vehicles parked near or around the hangar, any kind of parked vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps there were a number of vehicles parked in front, but I really cannot be sure about it. As for your previous question, of course there were members of the JNA in front of the hangar and in the hangar itself, just to complete that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It's not a question of completing the answer. I was not asking you about members of the JNA; I was asking you solely about members of the Territorial Defence. But let us continue. You said that in the hangar you saw Stanko Duvnjak and Milan Grezo. Is this correct? Should I repeat my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You don't need to repeat it, but we need to go back to this question. The JNA included the Territorial Defence, so you are depriving the Chamber of a reasonable answer. All the members within the JNA -- amongst the members of the JNA were also those from the Territorial Defence. You cannot really separate the Territorial Defence from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have to intervene. I am not able to turn my microphone on at any point because of you and your security. You asked for protective measures, and of course I fully respect that. But what I would like to ask you is when I am putting the question to you, please respond to that question. The Trial Chamber, if it has any problems in understanding either my question or your answer, I would assure you that the Trial Chamber will intervene. And if I put any impermissible questions, they will take steps to prevent that. So what I would like to ask you is to respond to my questions briefly so that I don't have to interrupt you, because I do not wish to endanger in any way the protective measures that were granted to you. Sir, you said that at a certain point you and another group of people were taken out of the hangar. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I appreciate your efforts to respect the protective measures, but I still have enough room to respond to you. Some of your statements are weird and strange and some things are not fully expressed. So this is why I'm telling you things that make sense. I'm not going to skip over any questions, and I will respond in the best possible way and in good will.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. In any case, I will be completing my cross-examination of you in another ten minutes. Can we go back to my question then. You said that at a certain point you and a group of about 10 or 20 people came out of the hangar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I came out, but I was brought out still. The questions put before that have not been clarified fully, especially when we're talking about Stanko Grezo [as interpreted] and Milan Duvnjak [as interpreted]. That was the purpose, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I don't have to tell you what the purpose of the question is. I put a question to you, you did not respond to that question, and now I move to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Let us not be confused, Ms. Tapuskovic. You asked a question. The witness said: Before I deal with that question, you haven't let me answer the one before that fully, and he dealt with the question before it. He hasn't yet turned to your last question. It's not that he's refused to answer it; he hasn't reached it. So if you want to get an answer from him about it, I think you should put it again. But if you're happy to leave it as it is, by all means, move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to avoid any kind of misunderstanding or any kind of tension, especially remarks by the witness while my microphone was on because I wanted to keep his identity confidential. What I did say to the witness is that I was not going to put any questions on that topic anymore. So I apologise if it was taken as my attempt to confuse the witness; that was not my intention. I simply said that I was not going to put that question anymore. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I was worried that you were confused about what the witness had answered and hadn't answered. I see you're very clear what is going on, so I will be quiet again and you carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I accept your correction. You said that you and a group of 10 to 20 people were brought out of the hangar. Do you agree with me that, according to what you said here, groups were taken out in intervals of about 20 minutes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was stated before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you were in the third group. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the third.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: But it was certainly not the first or the last group, was it, the people who you say were led outside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't the first group. I can't say about the last. Those who know could probably tell you. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On your way out of the hangar, there were quite many people remaining inside. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you were leaving the hangar, were you in the same group with those other people and was the group arranged in the shape of a column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was in that group, as you suggest. That is beyond doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where exactly were you in that column? Were you at the head? Were you somewhere around the middle? Or were you at the rear?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the rear of the column, as I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It would seem then that you headed from the hangar straight to that vehicle which you eventually boarded, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just I. The entire group of people. We were being led or directed towards that vehicle that was waiting outside the hangar.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You're quite right. When I said "you," I meant the entire group. There's a distinction in our language, as you know, but you have interpreted my question correctly. Tell me about this vehicle that you boarded. Did the vehicle have its headlights on at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is not that detailed. I don't know about the headlights, but I assume they would have been switched on already because it was dark by this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How long did it take for your group to leave the hangar and then for you personally to board that vehicle, since you say that you were towards the rear of that column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It only took a very brief time, a minute or two perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So after you boarded the vehicle, the tarp came down, the tarp was lowered, the tarpaulin, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The tarpaulin was not lowered. It was mounted on that vehicle and nothing at all was lowered.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken. I know about the tarpaulin being there, but as you and your group were boarding that vehicle, the section of the tarpaulin closing the entrance, was that lowered? Was the opening no longer free, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tarpaulin was never touched. It was the same way as when the vehicle first came. The tarpaulin makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Tell me something else about your way from the hangar to the vehicle. Did you perhaps notice that the same vehicles that you mentioned a while ago were parked around the area or were those vehicles no longer there or were there new vehicles in the area now? Do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I just remember the military vehicle. They were waiting for us to board. That's all I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I'll just have to look to see if I have any questions left for you. Sir, just one more thing. As far as we're able to tell, you have provided a total of 12 different statements to a number of different institutions and organisations since these events. Aside from what you were told by my learned friend from the OTP and Mr. Vasic, did you give any other statements to any other institutions or organisations concerning the events in Vukovar and at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you said it yourself, didn't you? You said "several different statements." I have no idea what you have in mind. What do you want to know about particularly?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I asked you about what you were told about. While testifying in chief my learned friend from the OTP enumerated all the statements that you gave, and you answered in the affirmative, didn't you? He was followed by my learned friend Mr. Vasic who asked you about two or three of the statements you made, and again you confirmed. I know that this is an enormous amount of evidence and documents. I do not wish to go to any length to examine this issue now. I do not wish to go back to the dates or places that these statements or given at. I don't wish to talk about the institutions that these statements were given to. All I want to know about is whether you can still remember if there were other statements that you gave to yet another institution or organisation, something that the three of us who had been asking you questions so far, have omitted or simply do not know about, something that we haven't referred to, that none of us have referred to? Just a yes or no, please, it really makes no difference.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just timing my answer. I don't know the exact number. When a statement was mentioned that I remember giving, I confirmed. What the form of the statement was, now that's very difficult to say and there should be records kept somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. Clearly, Mr. Bulatovic, the witness and you would enjoy a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume just after a quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon -- or rather, good evening to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Good evening to the witness. My name is Momcilo Bulatovic, one of Mr. Sljivancanin's Defence counsel. I will be asking you questions on behalf of our team. All the instructions that you received from my learned friends still apply. My understanding is you gave a whole lot of statements. My colleague Ms. Tapuskovic said you gave 12 statements. You testified several times. I went through your statements. I followed your testimony today and yesterday. My conclusion is you never actually met Mr. Sljivancanin in person, as they say, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not see him anywhere throughout the time in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we can agree that you did not see him on the 19th of November, 1991, at the hospital when you arrived. You did not see him on the 20th of November. You did not see him anywhere, not any of the places, where you were present, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't see him. You can count the minutes, the days, and the months. I didn't see him. That should suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. You state that there was an attempted break-through, an attempt to break through the lines, and you found out at one point that Vukovar's command had left Vukovar. So you advised your own people to try and break out. Isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true. I didn't say that there was an attempt to break out. We were left without our command. Our command abandoned their position and, in a way, this also left me demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What did you tell your own people after this occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say you have gone through my statements and studied them closely, then you should know that in a way I informed them of what had happened. As I described, I told them to do what they saw fit. I told them to leave town if they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This group -- or rather, your men, were these people natives of Vukovar, locals, or were they people who originally came from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were people from Vukovar in my unit, but there were people from other parts of Croatia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which other parts of Croatia, could you specify, please, and how many people who were not originally from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were several such people in my group. I should need to count them. Is it that important for you? If so, perhaps you can give me some time to collect my thoughts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not so much after their names, to be quite honest, but if you could specify their number, I mean the people who were not from Vukovar and who were members of your group, I would greatly appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've just repeated the same question, and what I'm telling you is I would need more time. I would need to look at my list. But the list was provided in my previous statements and it is clear, if you look at the lists, who came from where.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let's try to simplify this. Can you express yourself in terms of percentage in relation to your group. What percentage of men in your group were originally not from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Between 20 and 30 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you meant when you said that having found out that the command had left you assigned a local man to your group so that he could lead them out of the town of Vukovar. Why would that have been necessary if, according to your account, the people from Vukovar in your unit made up as much as 60 or 70 per cent of your entire unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 60 to 70 per cent that you referred to was a figure that was valid for as long as the unit was intact, but there were casualties. There were members of our unit who were killed somewhere along the way. Some were seriously wounded and were at the hospital. So the group dwindled, and these facts can be misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's try to turn this around because we seem to be creating unnecessary confusion. On the day when you realised that you were left without a command, to put it that way, how many men were there in your unit? How many men did it comprise on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now that I try to think back, there were two men who were from somewhere around Nasice, but on the day when the town was about to fall, there were some men there who were members of the National Guards Corps, defenders. And they formed a rather large group that was about to try and get out of Vukovar. They requested assistance from our unit. They wanted us to help them find the easiest way out since we were the unit that had laid all the minefields. They believed that in this way it would be easier for them to break through the lines and reach free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that they needed help, they needed to be taken through the minefields that you laid down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only that. They needed help generally because these were people who didn't know the layout of the town. They were in a new environment there, so they didn't get around so well. They were disoriented in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information, do you know whether there were also foreigners amongst the people who were defending the town of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the combat, in that period, I really don't know if there were any foreigners or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were at the hospital from the 19th until the 20th in the morning and when you were moving about the hospital, did you hear whether there were any members of the Croatian forces in the hospital who were wounded and who were foreign nationals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Now we're going to go back to the events from July and August 1991 which you already talked about, specifically about taking children and women away from Vukovar. What I would like to know is: Do you know how this was organised? Was this done through some kind of public proclamation? How was this organised and who organised it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did talk about that earlier, but it wasn't clear how this was done. What I do know is that this was organised by the HDZ. I don't know how this was done. I can't really tell you. That was done by using buses. They used buses to take the women and the children away, but I can't really give you any more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have information that some other organisations and the Catholic church participated in this action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information. I told you all I knew that this was organised, in a way, by the HDZ. I don't know whether there were other organisations that also participated in this. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you any more questions, since you don't know. But the evacuation that you mentioned when you were responding to questions by my learned friend Ms. Tapuskovic, that you heard that there was supposed to be an evacuation. What I would like to know is how you heard that. Did you hear it through the media, through the radio, by way of a proclamation or some other kind of informing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure how I found out about it. It's possible even that my father went to the hospital or a little bit further away and that he actually brought back this information, but I'm really not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Before you came to the hospital, did you have information that civilians would be taken to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You never heard from anyone that civilians were to be evacuated through Velepromet, that Velepromet was supposed to be used as a collection point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- well, I don't even know who would have been able to tell us something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that your recollection about these events was much fresher in March 1993 than it is today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have any thoughts about that. What I remember, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: In March 1993 did you talk with Canadian investigators? This is something that my learned friend from the Prosecution also reminded you of. Do you remember an interview that you had with this investigator?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did provide a statement to Canadian investigators, but I really don't remember exactly when this was. I did provide a statement to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I will remind you of a portion of that statement. We do have a transcript of that interview of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For my learned friends from the Prosecution, it's ERN 00596064, that's the page that I'm looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Your response is as follows to a question from the Canadian investigators. I'm going to read it. If you're not quite sure that I'm reading it correctly, I will also give you the transcript to read back. I'm reading your response. "News was disseminated that we would be going to Velepromet from the hospital and then again Velepromet as a collection centre." Do you recall you said this to the Canadian investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. I probably said that, but you asked me whether I knew before I went to the hospital that we would be going through Velepromet, that we would be leaving town via Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't want you to think that I was confusing you. I will put the question in this way. When you got to the hospital, did you hear then that civilians were supposed to go to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you boarded the buses in the way you described in front of the Vukovar Hospital, you said that no one told you where you were going. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I boarded one bus, not buses, and it's true that nobody told us where we were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you physically were not able to board more than one bus, but what I meant was everyone who was there. But since you want to be as specific as possible, I'm going to be as specific as you like. So no one told you who were boarding that one bus where you were going. My question is as follows: The soldiers who were guarding the bus that you were in, did you ask those soldiers where they were taking you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any of the other people who were on the bus with you ask the soldiers where they were taking you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask anyone -- ask anyone where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you set off from the barracks, you still didn't know where you were going. So what I am asking you is: Did you ask anyone then where you were going when you left the barracks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were asked about enemy soldiers, as you put it, by which you implied the Yugoslav People's Army and all the military structures that were, let's say, on that side. Do you recall providing a statement in Zagreb on the 20th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that you're thinking of my first statement after being released from captivity?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That's the statement I have. I don't know if there are any others. The one that I have bears the date 28th [as interpreted] of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the point of that question then?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just one intervention for the transcript, on page 61, line 19, it's not the 28th of August, it's the 20th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that in that statement that you provided in 1992 you mentioned a person with the nickname Capalo as being amongst the regular and the reserve JNA soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned that person because -- I just thought that that could be that person. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that in that statement you described that as a person that was short, with a beard, wearing a camouflage uniform, can we agree that that is how you described that person in your statement that you provided in August 1992, on the 20th of August, to be specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still see that person the way I saw them that day. But I no longer am quite sure about the nickname, but I assume that that person was taking part in the attack on Vukovar and was somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was exactly my next question. Was that person from Vukovar or from the environs of Vukovar? Do you know that person from Vukovar from before the war broke out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that person, but based on stories about certain people, I sort of concluded that that could be the person. But this is not something that I can be certain about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you were questioned at the district court in Zagreb on the 27th of April, 2004, in the presence of the deputy prosecutor for war crimes from Belgrade as well as the investigating judge from Belgrade, in response to questions about whom you know from Vukovar, and this question was put to you by the investigating judge from Belgrade, Mr. Alimpic, you said, among other things , I'm going to read to you again. If you doubt the veracity of what I'm reading, I will let you read it. But you said the following: "I also know Mirko Vojinovic, known as Capalo." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall saying that that was Mirko Vojinovic, Capalo. I don't remember saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about something else, so we're not going to waste any more time on this. Tell me the following: In response to questions from my learned friend Ms. Tapuskovic you said that you could not tell the difference in the JNA between the reserve soldiers, volunteers, members of the paramilitary formations, and regular soldiers because of the similarity of their uniforms, the camouflage uniforms, the olive-drab uniforms, and so on. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The group that the witness couldn't tell the difference between was slightly more limited than I think was put in the question. I believe he said he couldn't tell the difference between the reservists and paramilitary formations or the reservists and Territorial Defence, but not the number of groups that's been placed in that question. That's my recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm quickly trying to turn back. My own recollection is that it was a more restricted group than you have suggested, Mr. Bulatovic. Are you -- do you disagree with that? If so, we'll have to find the exact passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's how I understood it. It's possible that I am mistaken. Well, let's not waste any more time. Let's address the witness and then we can resolve that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... differentiate between reserve forces and Chetniks was the note I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honour, that's at page 48, lines 1 and 2, and 47, line 25, the last line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Was my note reliable or wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Oh. I've had one win this week. I think you might go a step back and just find out what he couldn't differentiate between, Mr. Bulatovic, and move from there, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Here's a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Could you clearly distinguish between what I shall call regular JNA soldiers on the one hand and all the other units that he observed in the area? If so, based on what?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very outlandish chapter of our conversation, sir. I'm not sure why distinction -- any distinction at all should be drawn between all these. It was all a unified environment, to be placed under one heading only with no particular distinctive features.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This precisely is the reason I am asking. Can you explain to us and the Trial Chamber the following: If you were able to distinguish between all these enemy forces and units, based on what? If not, please explain why.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is what constitutes the difficulty here. How can one explain who was a member of any of the units there. I wasn't able to know. I wasn't able to check. I wasn't able to ask which unit they belonged to. The only way was to try to distinguish based on their appearance, and that was probably not the most reliable way to ascertain their membership of any armed unit or perhaps based on their behaviour, what they were wearing. But the entire exercise would have been misleading. I wasn't well placed to draw an assured distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember how many people you saw at Ovcara inside or outside the hangar wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't say. I can't say if there was a single person wearing camouflage uniform. It's really difficult to answer questions like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about external features, based an which you would have been able to distinguish regular soldiers from those others, do you think age could be included as one of the possible factors of distinction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could have been helpful in a limited way. If you saw a young man wearing a regular uniform, they were likely to be regular soldiers, conscripts of the JNA. And those who were older could have been members of the TO or another unit that had been mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about this age issue. Where would you draw the line? What would be -- what would be the line that you would draw between the regular forces on the one hand and the TO on the other, what specific age?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone over 20 years of age would be more likely to be a member of the reserve forces, the kind usually called to military drills. That is not the sort of thing that you would expect an 18 year old or a 19 year old to be involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, if one of the people you saw there wearing a uniform the way you remembered them, and this person happened to be over 20 or over 30 years of age the way you reckoned, which unit would you have guessed them to be a member of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might have been TO, they might have been paramilitaries, they might have been Chetniks, they might have been from one of the volunteer units, they might have been from any of those units who joined at one point in time. There was a wide range of units present in the area on the enemy side. It was clear, however, that the JNA enjoyed the support of an external factor, but they were in control of the entire thing and they were the unifying element, to put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: My question wasn't about that, but I'm still happy with the answer you've given. Let me ask you this: During your time inside the hangar, did you see any member of these military units lead any of the detainees outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please say -- or rather, can you describe the circumstances, who was led away and under what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "circumstances," but to name a few. Sinisa Glavasevic was one of those who were led away, as well as another defender called Gaso. Those were the people I recognised. I'm not sure what else you think I could help you with.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did you notice if these people were returned or brought back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I want to know about that vehicle. A while ago in answer to one of the questions by Ms. Tapuskovic you said that the vehicle was driven up to the hangar, if my understanding is correct. If not, please explain how it got to be there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The vehicle was parked there. It had been driven up just before we were taken outside. It was waiting for us with the engine on and ready to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean by "parked," specifically in relation to the door, the hangar door? Did it back up to the door or was it parked in that street that ran parallel to the side of the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was there on the path connecting the road to the hangar. It wasn't at the door itself. Had it been at the door itself, we would not have been able to get out to begin with. There was some room between the hangar door and the truck itself, two, three, four metres perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this lorry was backed up to the hangar door and you boarded from the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The lorry had been driven up in reverse and the back of the lorry was facing the hangar door.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: This daylight, as it were, or the room which you crossed to reach the back of the lorry, my learned friend Ms. Tapuskovic asked you something about this but I don't think I understood your answer. Was the back of the lorry covered or closed with anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a bit of misunderstanding there, wasn't there? The vehicle was covered with tarpaulin, but the front side of the vehicle was open. And once everybody had boarded the vehicle, the steps were pulled up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe there's an error in the transcript on page 67, line 24. We talked about the front side of the vehicle, but actually I think the witness said the back of the vehicle -- or rather, the middle part of the vehicle. Maybe I should bring this up with the witness because there appears to be some confusion about this, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which part of the vehicle was open?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The middle part of the military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Which is the middle part?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The part where you get on. The middle part of the part where you get on towards the rear. How should I put it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Left side or right side?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The middle is the middle. The middle is precisely what it says. There is no left or right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid we're finding it slightly difficult to understand each other here. At the outset I even believed for a while that everything was crystal clear, but it now appears the situation is slightly confusing, therefore I will have to ask again. This part of the vehicle where you boarded, was it covered with tarpaulin or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the vehicle was covered. Apart from the part of the vehicle where we boarded which was partly covered, but the part where -- that was used for boarding was open, like I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: That means the back of the vehicle where you boarded had been driven up to the hangar door, and that part was open, the back of the vehicle, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was partly open, only as much was necessary for people to board, but that part, too, was covered with tarp.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The back of the vehicle where you boarded, how large was the opening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About one-third of the entire area, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I now fully understand. Once you boarded the vehicle, did you perhaps notice that there were other vehicles driving behind you or ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not able to see what was ahead of us, but I was able to see what was behind us, and there was nobody following.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone else but you try to jump off the vehicle? Did anyone entertain ideas of escape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've said that already, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you should ask them, not me. But this person that I have in mind is among the victims. However, there was this other man who was trying to scare him in a way and kept him from leaping off.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Why was this person scaring him? What was this person telling him? Did you hear an explanation of sorts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps "scaring" is not the right word. Rather, this other person was cautioning him not to do it because everybody would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: There's something I forgot to ask you. I hope you don't mind. Inside the hangar at Ovcara there was a length of rope you say used to separate something. What I want to know is how exactly was this length of rope positioned inside the hangar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was near the entrance to the hangar, near the green school-desk that I mentioned. I'm not sure what this length of rope was used for, but it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was it to the left or to the right on the way into the hangar in relation to the entrance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right in continuation, as I said, near the entrance, a bit more to the right, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know its purpose, what its purpose was, why this length of rope was left there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've answered that, haven't I? I didn't know the purpose, but it was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Was it used to separate groups of people, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been. I don't know. I'm not able to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a school-desk, a table. Did you see anyone seated at that desk writing something down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anyone writing anything down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Your name was recorded by a soldier that you described to the Canadian investigators, rather short, a thin moustache, but that's not what I want to know. How far was that the place where your details were taken from the desk that you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how far was the desk from me or the person taking my details?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: The person taking your details.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: 15 to 20 metres, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You said something about the number of mines you laid. In answer to one of the questions by Ms. Tapuskovic after she had shown you your statement to the Belgrade court, you said something about 40.000 mines, whereas in your testimony you say that your group only laid as many as 1.000. What I want to know is: Had mines been laid there before you came along in order to block or booby-trap certain areas, certain axes, groups before you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness didn't testify that he laid 40.000 mines. That statement was made in some testimony that he gave in Belgrade, and then he explained that the number wasn't necessarily accurate but it related to the general magnitude of mines being laid. And he certainly didn't say that his group laid 40.000 mines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's not suggested in the question, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At the beginning of the -- in a sense, yes. In the beginning of the question it said: You said something about the number of mines you laid. And then: "Ms. Tapuskovic showed a statement and you said something about 40.000 mines," implying that the witness said in that statement that he laid 40.000 mines. And in any event, he never agreed to that amount but said: Look, it was just a figure to reflect the magnitude of some minelaying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we're all aware of that and, above all else, the witness has kept a very clear head on some of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So I think you can proceed, Mr. Bulatovic. Thank you. The question being put to you, sir, was whether mines had been laid before you came along.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, someone had been laying mines before we came along. As I said, I only joined later on after the clashes had already broken out. It would be ridiculous for me to say that no one had been doing anything there before we came, but I'm not sure what the point of the question is or how I could possibly help with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I continue, Your Honour? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: So there had been someone laying mine before you came along. This is the reason I'm asking the question. Can we agree that those who had been laying mines before you came along, as you said those might have been members of MUP or some other units, had laid many more mines than you did later on. When you testified before the military court in Belgrade as an accused, the figure of 40.000 mines was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that I took charge of one of the units doing that kind of work. It's not difficult to assume that mines had been laid before I arrived on the scene. The other thing you're suggesting is just to give an idea of how far this went and that the number of mines actually laid might have been far greater than those that we eventually managed to set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What is the explosive charge of a single anti-tank mine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that this is at least five kilos of explosives, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Tapuskovic asked you about Vladimir Djukic. She also asked you about any information and knowledge you had concerning the existence of anti-aircraft guns or any such units, and you said you had no information whatsoever on that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've just said it. I said that, didn't I?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just checking if my understanding is correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it is. I said what I said. I did not know of any such units, units with that sort of a job or mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When talking to the Canadian investigators in March 1993 on page 4332 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for my friends 00596089.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: You were explaining to the investigators who Vladimir Djukic was and this is your answer. I'll read it out for you if you think I'm fabricating. Perhaps you can have a go yourself. "He was a commander over at Sajmiste. He was a commander of the anti-aircraft guns there." Do you remember stating this to the Canadian investigators, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in so many words. I don't think he could have been. He was at a command post and he had a weapon that was taken off a tank. The so-called PAM anti-aircraft machine-gun, but he wasn't there for the reasons that you are suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting anything. I am just reading a portion of your own statement. Let's move on. What about your brother? Was he involved in the fighting in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, maybe it might be a good idea to go into private session for this question. I'll ask about the person's name, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can just interject for a brief moment, Your Honour, it's a little bit belated, but it's in relation to Vladimir Djukic. And I think the proposition was put to the witness that he was the -- in charge of and in command of the anti-aircraft gun. I'm not really disputing that maybe that's the case somewhere in the statement. But on 00596089 all that we see is that he was a commander of the unit at Sajmiste. And it's not on that page, but bearing in mind we're not going to be introducing the statements to Court. I'm just wondering whether that statement, if that could be -- if we could be told of that and then we could agree to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was using the B/C/S. It's 34, page 34, and the number is 00596089. And indeed, if we look at line 9 we can see the witness's answer, the one I read out. He was a commander over at Sajmiste, a commander of the anti-aircraft guns. If there's anything else in any other transcript, I really don't know, but this is all I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We're not really in a position to dispute that at the moment. It appears that we have the B/C/S and the English on the same page, but it appears that the English hasn't been fully translated because it is said it was inaudible, but we accept Defence's statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just another question to finish up. The witness confirmed today that he never saw Mr. Sljivancanin personally. He said he saw him in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: What I want to ask the witness is: Which media? Where did he watch Mr. Sljivancanin or see Mr. Sljivancanin? How often? And is there anything that struck you as distinctive in the footage you saw, and which period of time are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a whole lot of questions. If you can please try to be a bit clearer and more precise. This is the marketplace style question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: If that's what you think of this courtroom, then that may influence my view of you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, not this courtroom, merely your questions, Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as we speak, I am part of this courtroom, or at least that's how I see myself. Nonetheless, I apologise. I will try to ask a really brief question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Where did the witness watch or see Mr. Sljivancanin, which mass media?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After my release, after the 14th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Were these recordings about Mr. Sljivancanin's time in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS P-011 [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BULATOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bulatovic. How does that place you, Mr. Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In the same place, no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You'll be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the questions that counsel have for you. And I think between counsel the various matters you felt you didn't get a chance to fully answer, you've managed to clear up. So the Chamber has no further questions for you. We would like to thank you for your time and trouble in coming here to The Hague and for the assistance that you have given us. When we rise in a few moments, you will be free to return to your home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before we rise, just so that counsel are aware of the position, the Chamber delayed giving our decision on a motion by Mr. Smith to admit into evidence, although only for the purpose of assessing the credibility of the witness, Mr. Vujic, a written statement that had been made by Slavko Tomic, who has since died. The basis for the motion of Mr. Smith was a question put to the witness by counsel for the accused Mr. Mrksic. That question, as it originally appeared in the English transcript, clearly indicated an attack on the credibility of the witness arising from his evidence as to the content of a conversation he'd had with Slavko Tomic. Because Mr. Vasic felt that as he remembered it he had not asked the question in the form that it appeared in the transcript, we delayed our decision and arranged to have the tape checked. That having been done, it is now apparent that the original transcript was misleading. Mr. Vasic's question did not call into question the credibility of the witness about the content of his conversation with Slavko Tomic. What Mr. Vasic asked was directed to a different conversation, one between Slavko Tomic and the accused Mr. Mrksic, a conversation which the witness did not hear. In these circumstances, there was no challenge to the credibility of the witness on this issue by Mr. Vasic. The statement will not, therefore, be admitted on the basis proposed. We will now adjourn, resuming on Monday at 2.15. And you, of course, are now free to go. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 13th day of March, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
